title: The Tale of the Educated Donkey
summary: A sly horse trader named Bhimsen brought a mangy grey donkey to the palace gates of Vijayanagara, claiming it was an 'Enlightened Scholarly Donkey' that had been educated by San...
keywords: the tale of the clever donkey trader
full_text:
A sly horse trader named Bhimsen brought a mangy grey donkey to the palace gates of Vijayanagara, claiming it was an 'Enlightened Scholarly Donkey' that had been educated by Sanskrit masters in Benares.
'This miraculous beast,' boasted Bhimsen to the curious courtiers, 'understands grammar and philosophy! When asked a profound question, it nods its head for truth and brays for falsehood!'

He demonstrated before a gullible courtier, asking: 'Is the Emperor the sun of righteousness?'
The donkey nodded its head eagerly up and down.
The courtier was so enchanted that he offered two hundred gold coins to buy the 'scholarly beast'.

Tenali Raman intervened:
'Wait, noble courtier! Let me examine the donkey’s mastery of the Vedas before you spend your gold.'

Tenali asked Bhimsen: 'May I ask the scholar three philosophical questions in private?'
Bhimsen reluctantly agreed.

Tenali took the donkey behind a screen in the courtyard.
He did not ask philosophical questions.
He took a handful of dry, roasted chickpeas—which donkeys love above all foods—and held it two inches above the donkey's nose.
The hungry donkey stretched its neck and nodded its head vigorously up and down to reach the food!
Tenali gave it one chickpea.
Then Tenali took a bundle of sharp, bitter wild thorn twigs and thrust it near the donkey’s lips.
The disgusted donkey tossed its head back, pinned its ears, and let out an ear-splitting, furious bray:
*‘HEE-HAW! HAW-HAW-HAW!’*

Tenali smiled. He brought the donkey back before the King and the courtier:
'Now, let us test the donkey’s scholarship!'

Tenali asked: 'O Scholarly Donkey, does this courtier have more brains than an earthen pot?'
Tenali held his closed fist near the donkey's nose, with the scent of roasted chickpeas on his fingers.
The donkey immediately nodded its head vigorously up and down!

Tenali then asked: 'O Scholarly Donkey, will this trader ever tell the truth in his life?'
Tenali waved a bitter neem leaf near its whiskers.
The donkey brayed violently in anger:
*‘HEE-HAW! HAW-HAW!’*

Tenali turned to the laughing courtier:
'You see? The donkey nods for food and brays at bitter leaves!
A donkey is a gentle beast made to carry laundry and grain, not to debate philosophy. Whosoever believes that an animal can master grammar without years of human study is more foolish than the beast he buys!'

The courtier blushed, kept his two hundred gold coins, and thanked Tenali.
The dishonest trader was ordered to clean the royal stables for a month, learning that fraudulent claims cannot fool true wit.
moral: Gullibility that believes in absurd shortcuts to scholarship is cured by humorous exposure.
